raw_response:
I am sixty-eight this year, and my legs are not what they used to be. I have worked my 7.5 mu in Quzhou for twenty years, and I know every ridge and ditch. With five mouths to feed and my children working in town, I cannot afford big gambles. I keep the backbone of my farm in wheat-maize double-cropping on 4.5 mu. The wheat went in last October, and now that the greening season is here I will topdress urea at jointing and irrigate four times from my well—greening water, jointing water, heading water, and grain-filling water. After harvest in early June, I will sow hybrid maize directly without deep plowing; no-tillage saves my back and the moisture in the soil. The maize only needs two good irrigations if the summer rains are normal, and I expect a solid yield.

Vegetables earn more cash but they are back-breaking and risky. At my age, I limit myself to 3 mu of them. I have 1 mu of spring cabbage already in the nursery; I will rotary-till the plot, lay down compound fertilizer, and transplant in March. It should head up by May and sell before the summer glut. Chili gets 1 mu—transplanted in May, fed with extra potassium, watered five times, and sprayed often for aphids and virus. Eggplant gets the last 1 mu; it is profitable but the whiteflies and wilt are relentless, so I water six times and spray every ten days during fruiting. I buy improved seeds for wheat and hybrid seeds for maize and cabbage—the extra cost pays for itself. I do not keep livestock anymore, so I rely on chemical fertilizer from the cooperative: compound for the basal, urea for topdressing. My well never runs dry, so I irrigate when the crops need it, not when the sky decides.
